subject: ELA
title: English 10
description: A tenth-grade English course organized around world literature and the rhetoric of power, conflict, and freedom, paired with Modern World History. Students read short fiction, Greek and Shakespearean tragedy, Things Fall Apart, Night, Fahrenheit 451, A Doll's House, war poetry and landmark speeches. Every unit weaves close reading, grammar and vocabulary, discussion, and a major written product (narrative, literary analysis, argument, and a multi-source research paper).
framework: California Common Core State Standards for ELA/Literacy (grades 9–10); 2014 CA ELA/ELD Framework

standards.RL.9-10.1: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what a literary text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RL.9-10.2: Determine a theme of a literary text, analyze its development, and provide an objective summary.
standards.RL.9-10.3: Analyze how complex characters develop, interact, and advance the plot or develop the theme.
standards.RL.9-10.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases, including figurative language, and analyze the cumulative impact of word choice on meaning and tone.
standards.RL.9-10.5: Analyze how an author's choices about structure, order of events, and manipulation of time create mystery, tension, or surprise.
standards.RL.9-10.6: Analyze a particular point of view or cultural experience reflected in a work of literature from outside the United States.
standards.RL.9-10.7: Analyze the representation of a subject or key scene in two different artistic mediums.
standards.RL.9-10.9: Analyze how an author draws on and transforms source material in a specific work.
standards.RL.9-10.10: Read and comprehend literature, including stories, dramas, and poems, in the grades 9–10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
standards.RI.9-10.1: Cite strong and thorough textual evidence to support analysis of what an informational text says explicitly and by inference.
standards.RI.9-10.2: Determine a central idea of an informational text, analyze its development, and provide an objective summary.
standards.RI.9-10.3: Analyze how an author unfolds an analysis or series of ideas or events and the connections drawn between them.
standards.RI.9-10.4: Determine the meaning of words and phrases in informational text and analyze the cumulative impact of word choice on meaning and tone.
standards.RI.9-10.5: Analyze in detail how an author's ideas or claims are developed and refined by particular sentences, paragraphs, or sections.
standards.RI.9-10.6: Determine an author's point of view or purpose and analyze how rhetoric advances it.
standards.RI.9-10.7: Analyze various accounts of a subject told in different mediums, determining which details are emphasized in each.
standards.RI.9-10.8: Delineate and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, assessing reasoning and evidence and identifying false statements and fallacies.
standards.RI.9-10.9: Analyze seminal U.S. and world documents of historical and literary significance, including how they address related themes and concepts.
standards.RI.9-10.10: Read and comprehend literary nonfiction in the grades 9–10 text complexity band independently and proficiently.
standards.W.9-10.1: Write arguments to support claims using valid reasoning and relevant and sufficient evidence.
standards.W.9-10.2: Write informative/explanatory texts to examine and convey complex ideas clearly and accurately.
standards.W.9-10.3: Write narratives to develop real or imagined experiences using effective technique, well-chosen details, and well-structured event sequences.
standards.W.9-10.4: Produce clear and coherent writing appropriate to task, purpose, and audience.
standards.W.9-10.5: Develop and strengthen writing by planning, revising, editing, rewriting, or trying a new approach.
standards.W.9-10.6: Use technology, including the Internet, to produce, publish, and update individual or shared writing products.
standards.W.9-10.7: Conduct short and sustained research projects to answer a question or solve a problem, synthesizing multiple sources.
standards.W.9-10.8: Gather relevant information from multiple authoritative sources, assess usefulness, and integrate information while avoiding plagiarism and following a standard citation format.
standards.W.9-10.9: Draw evidence from literary or informational texts to support analysis, reflection, and research.
standards.W.9-10.10: Write routinely over extended and shorter time frames for a range of tasks, purposes, and audiences.
standards.SL.9-10.1: Initiate and participate effectively in collaborative discussions, building on others' ideas and expressing their own clearly and persuasively.
standards.SL.9-10.2: Integrate multiple sources of information presented in diverse media or formats, evaluating credibility and accuracy.
standards.SL.9-10.3: Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning, and use of evidence and rhetoric.
standards.SL.9-10.4: Present information, findings, and evidence clearly, concisely, and logically so listeners can follow the line of reasoning.
standards.SL.9-10.5: Make strategic use of digital media in presentations to enhance understanding.
standards.SL.9-10.6: Adapt speech to a variety of contexts and tasks, demonstrating command of formal English.
standards.L.9-10.1: Demonstrate command of grammar and usage, including parallel structure and various types of phrases and clauses.
standards.L.9-10.2: Demonstrate command of capitalization, punctuation, and spelling, including semicolons, colons, and conjunctive adverbs.
standards.L.9-10.3: Apply knowledge of language to make effective choices for meaning or style; write and edit work to conform to a style manual (MLA).
standards.L.9-10.4: Determine or clarify the meaning of unknown words using context, word parts (roots and affixes), and reference materials.
standards.L.9-10.5: Demonstrate understanding of figurative language, word relationships, and nuances in word meanings.
standards.L.9-10.6: Acquire and use accurately general academic and domain-specific words and phrases.

units.title: The Short Story: Craft and Suspense
units.big_idea: Writers manipulate structure, point of view and detail to create tension and meaning.

units.title: Greek Tragedy: Antigone
units.big_idea: Conflicts between individual conscience and state law are as old as drama.

units.title: Julius Caesar and the Power of Rhetoric
units.big_idea: Language can win crowds, topple leaders and justify violence.

units.title: Things Fall Apart: Colonialism and Culture
units.big_idea: A culture's story looks different when told from inside it.

units.title: Literature of War and Witness
units.big_idea: Testimony and poetry make the cost of war personal and unforgettable.

units.title: Rhetoric of Freedom: Research and Argument
units.big_idea: Seminal speeches and documents shaped how the modern world defines human rights.

units.title: Dystopia: Fahrenheit 451
units.big_idea: Societies that suppress ideas reveal what makes free thought valuable.

units.title: A Doll's House and Poetry of Identity
units.big_idea: Individuals push against the roles their societies assign them.

units.title: Portfolio, Reflection and Final Assessment
units.big_idea: Growth as a reader and writer is visible when you revisit and revise your work.

weeks.topic: Suspense and structure: 'The Most Dangerous Game'

days.title: Course launch & reading survey
days.work: Complete a reading-history survey, set up a reading journal, and write a one-page 'reader autobiography' as a writing baseline.

days.title: Read Connell, part 1
days.work: Read the first half of 'The Most Dangerous Game' and annotate every foreshadowing clue on Ship-Trap Island with sticky notes or margin marks.

days.title: Read Connell, part 2
days.work: Finish the story and chart the rising tension on a plot diagram, quoting one sentence for each stage.

days.title: Grammar: phrases
days.work: Identify prepositional, participial and appositive phrases in ten sentences from the story, then write five sentences imitating Connell's participial openers.

days.title: Summary & discussion
days.work: Write a 150-word objective summary (no opinion) and discuss with a parent: is Rainsford changed by the end? Cite two lines.

weeks.assessment: Objective summary scored for accuracy and no opinion; plot diagram with quoted evidence.

weeks.topic: Unreliable narrators: Poe's 'The Cask of Amontillado'
objectives: Analyze point of view and irony
Use textual evidence to infer motive

days.title: Read Poe
days.work: Read 'The Cask of Amontillado' aloud and highlight every instance of verbal irony in Montresor's speech to Fortunato.

days.title: Irony chart
days.work: Build a three-column chart (quote / what it says / what it really means) for six ironic moments, labeling each verbal or dramatic.

days.title: Word study: Latin roots
days.work: Study roots (ven-, mort-, cred-, jur-) from the story's vocabulary (impunity, immolation, retribution) and build a 12-word root web.

days.title: Analytical paragraph
days.work: Write a TIQA paragraph (topic, intro to quote, quote, analysis) answering: Is Montresor a reliable narrator? Cite two pieces of evidence.

days.title: Quiz & revise
days.work: Take a short quiz on irony and point of view, then revise the paragraph using teacher feedback on quote integration.

weeks.assessment: Analytical paragraph rubric (claim, evidence, analysis) and irony quiz.

weeks.topic: Time and twist: 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' and 'The Necklace'
objectives: Compare situational irony in two stories

days.title: Read Bierce
days.work: Read 'An Occurrence at Owl Creek Bridge' and mark where time slows, jumps back, and resumes; sketch a timeline of real vs. imagined time.

days.title: Film comparison
days.work: Watch the 1961 short film of Owl Creek Bridge (library/streaming) and list three choices the director made differently than Bierce (RL.9-10.7 preview).

days.title: Read Maupassant
days.work: Read 'The Necklace' and annotate details of 19th-century French class and status that drive Mathilde's choices.

days.title: Compare endings
days.work: Write a 250-word comparison of the twist endings: how does each author plant clues so the surprise feels earned?

days.title: Socratic discussion
days.work: Lead a 15-minute discussion with family on 'Which twist is more meaningful, and why?' using three prepared questions and evidence.

weeks.assessment: Comparison response scored on evidence and analysis of structure; discussion participation checklist.

objectives: Write an original short story using suspense techniques
Revise for pacing and dialogue punctuation

days.title: Plan the story
days.work: Brainstorm a 1,000–1,500 word suspense story and plan it on a plot mountain, choosing a narrator and one structural trick (flashback, twist, in medias res).

days.title: Draft opening
days.work: Draft the opening scene starting in medias res, using at least three sensory details and one foreshadowing clue.

days.title: Draft middle & end
days.work: Complete the draft, writing a climax scene where sentences shorten to speed pacing.

days.title: Revise & edit
days.work: Revise using a checklist (dialogue punctuation, varied sentence openers, show-don't-tell), then peer/parent-read aloud for confusing spots.

days.title: Publish & unit test
days.work: Type the final story in MLA format and take the Unit 1 test on literary terms and a cold-read short passage.

days.title: Greek theater background
days.work: Watch a short video on Greek theater (masks, chorus, Dionysia) and take Cornell notes on Aristotle's elements of tragedy.

days.title: Oedipus family backstory
days.work: Read a summary of the Theban myth and create a family tree of Oedipus, Jocasta, Antigone, Ismene, Polyneices, Eteocles and Creon.

days.title: Read Prologue
days.work: Read the Prologue aloud in two voices and chart how Antigone and Ismene differ in values, citing three lines each.

days.title: Read Parodos & Scene 1
days.work: Read the Parodos and Scene 1 and paraphrase Creon's opening speech on loyalty to the state.

days.title: Check & reflect
days.work: Take a reading-check quiz and write a journal entry: which law matters more, divine law or civic law?

objectives: Track the role of the chorus

days.title: Read Scene 2
days.work: Read Scene 2 (the confrontation) and annotate each rhetorical move Antigone and Creon make.

days.title: Stichomythia practice
days.work: Perform the rapid line exchange aloud with a partner and explain how the form heightens conflict.

days.title: Ode 2 & figurative language
days.work: Read Ode 2 and identify the extended metaphor of the curse as a storm; explain its effect in a short paragraph.

days.title: Read Scene 3 – Haemon
days.work: Read Scene 3 and evaluate Haemon's arguments to his father; list his three strongest points.

days.title: Quiz & journal
days.work: Complete a quiz on Scenes 2–3 and a journal entry on whether Creon is a tyrant or a ruler doing his duty.

weeks.topic: Antigone: Downfall and the tragic hero
objectives: Determine who is the tragic hero

days.title: Read Scenes 4–5
days.work: Read Antigone's farewell and Teiresias's warning; mark the moment Creon's reversal begins.

days.title: Exodos
days.work: Finish the play and complete a cause-effect chain from Creon's decree to the deaths.

days.title: Compare a staging
days.work: Watch one scene from a filmed production and compare how actors portray Creon versus your reading.

days.title: Seminar
days.work: Hold a Socratic seminar on 'Who is the tragic hero, Antigone or Creon?' using at least four cited lines.

days.title: Theme statement
days.work: Write three possible theme statements for the play and choose the strongest with a justification.

weeks.topic: Argument essay: Antigone and civil disobedience

days.title: Read Thoreau excerpt
days.work: Read an excerpt of Thoreau's 'Civil Disobedience' and note parallels with Antigone's position.

days.title: Outline
days.work: Outline an argument essay: Is Antigone right to break Creon's law? Include claim, two reasons, a counterclaim and rebuttal.

days.title: Draft
days.work: Draft the 700–900 word essay, integrating quotes from both the play and Thoreau.

days.title: Grammar: parallel structure
days.work: Mini-lesson on parallel structure; revise three sentences in your draft to use parallelism for emphasis.

days.title: Final draft & unit test
days.work: Submit the final essay and take the Unit 2 test on tragic conventions and vocabulary.

weeks.assessment: Argument essay rubric and Unit 2 test.

days.title: Act 3.1

days.title: Motive debate

days.title: Check
days.work: Quiz on Acts 2–3.1 and a timeline of the conspiracy.

weeks.topic: The funeral orations: rhetoric in action

days.title: Rhetorical appeals
days.work: Learn ethos/pathos/logos and identify each in three modern ads or speeches.

days.title: Brutus's speech
days.work: Analyze Brutus's prose oration for logos and parallel structure, marking each device.

days.title: Antony's speech
days.work: Analyze 'Friends, Romans, countrymen' tracking the repetition of 'honourable man' and how meaning shifts.

days.title: Performance
days.work: Memorize and perform 12–20 lines of Antony's speech with intentional pauses and emphasis.

days.title: Comparison response
days.work: Write a timed 40-minute response: Why does Antony's speech succeed where Brutus's fails?

objectives: Trace the fall of the conspirators

days.title: Act 4
days.work: Read the quarrel scene (4.3) and analyze how Brutus and Cassius's friendship unravels.

days.title: Act 5
days.work: Read Act 5 and record how each conspirator dies and what Antony says of Brutus.

days.title: Medium comparison
days.work: Compare the funeral scene in two film versions and write which interpretation is more persuasive.

days.title: Tragic hero
days.work: Decide whether Caesar or Brutus is the tragic hero, completing an Aristotelian criteria chart.

days.title: Test
days.work: Unit test on the play: passage identification, rhetoric analysis, and short essay.

objectives: Write and deliver a persuasive speech using rhetorical devices

days.title: Choose an issue
days.work: Choose a contemporary community issue and research two credible facts and one quotation to support a position.

days.title: Draft speech
days.work: Draft a 3–4 minute speech using at least anaphora, antithesis, a rhetorical question and a tricolon.

days.title: Revise for audience
days.work: Revise for audience and timing; mark the script for pauses and emphasis.

days.title: Rehearse
days.work: Rehearse twice on video and self-score eye contact, pace and volume.

days.title: Deliver
days.work: Deliver the speech to family and answer two audience questions.

weeks.topic: Things Fall Apart Part 1: Igbo society
objectives: Analyze cultural perspective in a non-U.S. novel

days.work: Read about Nigeria, the Igbo people and British colonization; locate Igboland on a map.

days.title: Ch. 1–4
days.work: Read chapters 1–4 and record Okonkwo's fears and their roots in his father Unoka.

days.work: Collect eight proverbs from the novel and explain what each reveals about Igbo values.

days.title: Ch. 5–8

days.title: Check

weeks.topic: Things Fall Apart Part 1 (cont.): Tradition and change
objectives: Analyze how characters develop through conflict

days.title: Ch. 9–10

days.title: Ch. 11–13

days.title: Vocabulary in context

days.title: Analysis paragraph

days.title: Discussion
days.work: Discuss with family: Which Igbo traditions does the novel present as strengths, and which as weaknesses?

days.title: Part 3

days.title: The ending
days.work: Analyze the District Commissioner's final paragraph: what is Achebe saying about who writes history?

days.title: Quiz
days.work: Quiz on Parts 2–3 and a cause-effect chart of colonial change.

weeks.topic: Literary analysis essay: Things Fall Apart

days.title: Choose prompt
days.work: Choose a prompt (e.g., How does Achebe use Okonkwo's fall to represent the fall of Umuofia?) and write a working thesis.

days.title: Evidence map
days.work: Gather eight quotations and map them to three body paragraphs.

days.title: Draft
days.work: Draft the 1,000-word essay with MLA in-text citations.

days.title: Grammar: semicolons & colons
days.work: Mini-lesson on semicolons, colons and conjunctive adverbs; add three correct uses to the draft.

days.title: Revise
days.work: Revise using a rubric and read the essay aloud to catch errors.

objectives: Demonstrate semester mastery in reading and writing

days.title: Final essay due

days.title: Review terms

days.title: Cold read practice

days.title: Semester exam
days.work: Take the semester exam: cold-read analysis, terms, grammar, and a timed argument essay.

days.title: Reflection
days.work: Write a semester reflection comparing your Week 1 writing sample to your Week 18 essay.

objectives: Analyze character and social roles in realist drama

days.title: Context
days.work: Read about 19th-century Norwegian society and women's legal status; note what Nora cannot do legally.

days.title: Act 1
days.work: Read Act 1 and chart Torvald's pet names for Nora and what they reveal.

days.title: Act 2
days.work: Read Act 2 and analyze the tarantella as a symbol.

days.title: Dramatic irony
days.work: List secrets audiences know that Torvald doesn't and explain the tension created.

days.title: Quiz
days.work: Quiz on Acts 1–2.

weeks.topic: A Doll's House Act 3 and poetry of identity
materials: Langston Hughes 'Let America Be America Again'
Rabindranath Tagore 'Where the Mind is Without Fear'

days.title: Act 3
days.work: Read Act 3 and analyze Nora's final speech line by line.

days.title: The door slam
days.work: Debate: Is Nora's leaving justified? Discuss the play's 1879 reception.

days.title: Tagore
days.work: Read Tagore's poem and connect its vision of freedom to Unit 6 speeches.

days.title: Hughes & McKay
days.work: Read Hughes and McKay poems and analyze form and tone.

days.title: Response
days.work: Write a comparative response: how do Nora and one poem's speaker claim identity?

objectives: Write original poems using figurative techniques

days.title: Imitation poem
days.work: Write an imitation of Tagore's structure ('Where…') about your own vision of freedom.

days.title: Extended metaphor
days.work: Write a poem built on one extended metaphor for identity.

days.title: Monologue
days.work: Write a 1-minute dramatic monologue for a minor character from any text this year.

days.title: Perform
days.work: Rehearse and perform the monologue or a poem for family.

days.title: Unit 8 check
days.work: Unit 8 test on drama and poetry terms with a cold-read poem.

weeks.assessment: Creative portfolio pieces and unit test.

days.title: Select pieces
days.work: Select three best pieces (narrative, analysis, argument/research) for a final portfolio.

days.title: Revise piece 1
days.work: Deeply revise one essay based on earlier feedback, tracking changes.

days.title: Revise piece 2
days.work: Revise a second piece for style: sentence variety, precise verbs, parallelism.

days.title: Reflective letter
days.work: Write a 600-word reflective letter explaining your growth as a reader and writer.

days.title: Publish
days.work: Publish the portfolio as a digital document or website.

days.title: Review
days.work: Review key texts and terms with a self-made study guide.

days.title: Practice exam
days.work: Complete a CAASPP-style practice performance task.

days.title: Final exam
days.work: Take the final: cold reads (literary and informational), grammar, and a timed argument essay.

days.title: Portfolio presentation
days.work: Present the portfolio in a 6-minute talk with slides.

days.title: Summer reading plan
days.work: Create a summer reading list of five books and set reading goals.
